Promising directions include ISR as a post-hoc filter (selecting high-ISR outputs without backpropagating through the metric), normalized variants that control for the premise-count confound, and hybrid rewards that combine execution feedback with semantic faithfulness signals independent of component-count structure.

\paragraph{STA generalization.}
While our experiments use FOL and Prolog, the STA protocol (LOO ablation on solver inputs) applies to any setting with a compositional input format and a binary verifier: SMT solvers, proof assistants, constraint satisfaction systems, and program synthesis with test suites.
The specific hacking modes will differ across domains, but the structural vulnerability of LOO-based metrics to low-component-count exploits follows from the metric definition and should transfer.
Applying STA to richer logics (e.g., higher-order, temporal) may require domain-specific component decomposition strategies.

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For practitioners building solver-backed RL systems: (1) use ISR or similar structural diagnostics for post-hoc evaluation, not as training signals; (2) report mode-level breakdowns alongside aggregate metrics, since ISR alone does not distinguish faithful derivation from metric gaming; (3) evaluate across multiple seeds and training horizons, since snapshot evaluation at a single checkpoint can overestimate structural quality by an order of magnitude.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for solver-backed formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts.
This gap is especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback, driving rapid prove-rate gains but providing no signal on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings; a separate line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}.
What is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in solver-backed formal outputs.

We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs to test whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
The fraction of necessary components yields the \emph{Irreducible Solver Rate} (ISR), where $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicates full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to prove rate: structural quality degrades by $99.5\%$ over 1000 steps while prove rate rises from $32\%$ to $96\%$ (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
An SFT baseline on identical data largely avoids hacking, consistent with the failure being RL-specific, though the large prove-rate gap prevents definitive causal attribution (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
The mechanism is structural: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive high ISR by construction, creating an attractor that eventually captures all seeds under extended training.
The effect transfers to Prolog with complete collapse through three distinct mechanisms (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

We present an empirical case study of Goodhart collapse in solver-backed RL, using FOLIO with Qwen3 (4B/1.7B) across six reward conditions, five seeds, two logic types, and up to 1000 training steps. Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{ISR as a structural diagnostic} for GRPO reward hacking, revealing a collapse trajectory invisible to prove rate (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
  \item \textbf{Empirical characterization of Goodhart dynamics} under LOO-based rewards, including seed-dependent divergence, dose-varying patterns, and a taxonomy of eight automatically detected hacking modes plus one identified by manual audit (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}--\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
  \item \textbf{Cross-logic extension} to Prolog with consistent Goodhart effects across all seeds (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
\end{enumerate}
These are cautionary results from a single model family and dataset: snapshot evaluation of structural rewards can overestimate their benefit; only trajectory analysis reveals the transient nature of apparent improvement.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), and ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}--\ref{sec:crossscale}).
At 500 steps, ISR produces descriptively more non-hacking output than random controls (Table~\ref{tab:goodhart-landscape}), but seed-level permutation tests are underpowered ($n{=}5$), and the advantage reverses under stricter classification.
Extended training confirms the window closes.
The core asymmetry is clear: the same LOO structure that makes ISR a useful diagnostic also makes it a vulnerable optimization target, because tautological constructions satisfy component necessity by definition.
While Goodhart collapse under LOO-based metrics is theoretically predictable, the specific dynamics resist prediction from the metric definition alone: seed-dependent divergence, dose-varying collapse patterns, and cross-logic mode divergence each required empirical observation to identify.

All experiments use a single model family (Qwen3-4B/1.7B), one dataset (FOLIO), and one RL algorithm (GRPO).
The specific hacking modes and their relative prevalence may differ under other architectures or formal reasoning benchmarks, but the structural vulnerability of LOO-based metrics to tautological exploits follows from the metric definition and should transfer to any setting where the optimizer can reduce component count.
Our results illustrate a concrete instance of Goodhart's law in RL for formal reasoning~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: the failure mode is regressional rather than extremal, with the optimizer concentrating probability mass on regions where ISR's structural bias coincides with degenerate outputs.
For scalable oversight of solver-backed systems, structural diagnostics should remain decoupled from the training loop.

The STA protocol (LOO ablation on solver inputs) applies beyond FOL and Prolog to any setting with a compositional input format and a binary verifier, including SMT solvers, proof assistants, and program synthesis with test suites.
TRACE~\citep{wang2025trace}, which detects reward hacking by measuring reasoning effort, provides a complementary diagnostic axis; combining structural necessity (STA) with effort-based detection (TRACE) may yield more robust hacking identification than either alone.
For practitioners, we recommend using ISR for post-hoc evaluation rather than as a training signal, reporting mode-level breakdowns alongside aggregate metrics, and evaluating across multiple seeds and training horizons to avoid overestimating structural quality from snapshot evaluations.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Experiments use a single model family (Qwen3-4B/1.7B), a single structured-NLI dataset (FOLIO, 500 training examples and 100 evaluation examples), and a single RL algorithm (GRPO).
Whether the specific hacking modes and collapse dynamics generalize to other architectures or larger-scale formal reasoning benchmarks remains open.
Our 1.7B experiments use three seeds per condition; strict non-hacking rates range from $0$--$3.7\%$ (ISR $\beta{=}0.1$) to $0$--$29\%$ (ISR $\beta{=}0.3$, driven by a single low-PR seed), and $N{=}3$ may miss rare non-hacking-capable initializations.
The automated classifier does not detect H9 (ex falso) at 1.7B; manual audit found H9 instances within taxonomy-classified categories, so 1.7B non-hacking rates may overestimate true rates.

ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a high-ISR proof can still be logically vacuous if its individually necessary premises are collectively inconsistent or semantically ungrounded.
A downstream NLI evaluation confirms this gap ($\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
The current decomposition treats conclusion sub-expressions (quantifier, antecedent, consequent) as separate components; for tautological formulas where sub-expressions overlap with premises, ISR values can depend on decomposition granularity rather than proof structure, though these edge cases do not affect aggregate statistics.
Non-hacking is a residual classification: undiscovered gaming modes would reduce the true rate, as illustrated by H7b (obfuscated tautology evading text-match classifiers) and query-as-fact gaming in Prolog.
STA requires solvers supporting component-level input manipulation, adding $O(n)$ solver calls per sample (mean $n{\approx}6$--$8$ in our experiments, ${\sim}6$--$8{\times}$ evaluation overhead); at training time with ISR reward, this overhead applies to all proved rollouts per GRPO step.

Five seeds demonstrate qualitative divergence but limit statistical power for seed-level permutation tests ($p{\geq}0.26$; minimum achievable $p{=}0.008$ at $n{=}5$).
CMH tests yield $p{<}10^{-9}$ but assume within-stratum independence, which is violated when samples share a checkpoint and decoding strategy; CMH $p$-values should be interpreted as directional indicators, not calibrated significance levels.
Dose coverage is sparse: ISR $\beta{=}0.05$ and $\beta{=}0.2$ each use three seeds, the primary $\beta{=}0.1$ comparison uses five, and qualitative differences across doses should be treated as preliminary observations.
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ s43 and s44 checkpoints were lost during disk cleanup, preventing retrospective H8 audit; the reported 5-seed pooled non-hacking rate (23\%) is an uncorrected upper bound.
We report individual $p$-values without correction for multiple comparisons; given the exploratory nature and limited seed counts, reported $p$-values are descriptive rather than confirmatory.
All 500-step results are temporal snapshots: trajectory analysis (1000 steps) confirms that the non-hacking window under ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ is transient (s42: $17\%{\to}2\%$; s45: $55\%{\to}0\%$), and 500-step non-hacking rates should be interpreted as upper bounds on long-run structural quality.
